decisions.approvalNote: User approved Option A and clarified that the guided experience should reuse the established ordered-steps visual pattern from Dataset Preparation and Model Training, with plain-language primary steps and progressive disclosure for advanced controls.
decisions.context: The choice determines whether the roadmap primarily reorganizes the user experience around a guided outcome, preserves the current technical forms, or exposes a configurable data-engineering pipeline. All options include the immediate correctness, compatibility, privacy, split-integrity, and diagnostic fixes; they differ in product structure, terminology, flexibility, and implementation scope.

consequences: Users choose goals and see readiness, warnings, samples, and recommended actions instead of configuring data-engineering internals first.
The system can enforce one end-to-end capability contract and refuse misleading format, split, or destination choices before work starts.
Dataset versions, quality reports, lineage, and publication documentation become normal outputs rather than optional expert tasks.
The roadmap is a larger modernization, delivered through a few independently useful increments with compatibility-preserving rollback.
options.label: Option A — Guided data workflow
options.summary: Create one plain-language journey—Add data, Check data, Prepare dataset, Review, and Publish—using sensible defaults, short explanations, previews, and an Advanced settings disclosure for technical controls. Preserve the accepted artifact/runtime architecture underneath, use a canonical streaming tabular representation for preparation, and make remote localization, profiling, curation, splitting, versioning, and dataset documentation part of the guided path.
tradeoffs: Best fit for non-technical users and the clearest way to prevent unsupported or unsafe combinations.
Requires coordinated contract, application, storage/provider, Python worker, desktop/thin-client, documentation, migration, and test work.
Advanced users retain detailed controls, but those controls move out of the primary path and may be grouped or renamed.

consequences: Correctness and security improve, but the product remains oriented toward technically experienced users.
Future features are likely to add more controls to already dense tabs.
A later UX restructuring would revisit many of the same components and tests.
options.label: Option B — Harden the existing tabs
options.summary: Keep the current Ingestion and Dataset Preparation forms and navigation, correct the split and format defects, add missing validation and quality controls, and improve labels/tooltips without materially changing the workflow structure.
tradeoffs: Smaller initial UI disruption and easier visual regression review.
Retains a long configuration form and makes users understand normalization, chunking, generation, split, format, and model controls before they can produce a dataset.
Quality review and publishing remain separate collections of controls rather than a guided outcome.

consequences: The Data Management area becomes a general data-orchestration product rather than a focused training-dataset workflow.
New persisted recipe, compatibility, execution-planning, versioning, and possibly distributed scheduling decisions would be required.
Delivery would take more increments and broaden beyond the current accepted runtime lifecycle constraints.
options.label: Option C — Visual pipeline builder
options.summary: Expose ingestion, normalization, profiling, filtering, generation, validation, splitting, and publication as user-configurable pipeline stages with reusable recipes and a graph or stage editor.
tradeoffs: Maximum flexibility, inspection, and extensibility for data engineers and research teams.
Highest implementation, migration, documentation, support, and accessibility cost.
Introduces substantial concepts and terminology that conflict with the requested non-technical default experience unless paired with a separate simplified mode.

decisions.approvalNote: User selected the adaptive direction and clarified that both primary choices and Advanced settings must respond to the exact training task, selected source kind, and preparation option without exposing ignored or contradictory controls.
decisions.context: Broad text-versus-image adaptation remains misleading because instruction tuning, classification, extraction, embedding, reranking, diffusion, image classification, detection, and segmentation require different fields, quality rules, example-creation actions, and review evidence. Document sectioning or topic-aware chunking is a source-processing method that should appear only when an unstructured textual source must be converted into examples.

consequences: Instruction tuning distinguishes existing instruction-answer examples from grounded example generation and verified alternatives.
Classification validates labels and balance; extraction validates expected outputs against a schema; embedding and reranking validate positive and negative relationships.
Diffusion, classification, detection, and segmentation show only the caption, label, box, or mask actions actually supported.
Document splitting is automatic by default and becomes a task-relevant advanced control only when source documents need conversion.
Common source association, license, consent, privacy, credential, duplicate, and split controls remain shared but report only the content surfaces they actually inspected.
options.label: Option A — Exact-task adaptive workflow
options.summary: Keep one four-step experience, but derive both data checks and example-creation choices from the exact selected training task and selected source capabilities.
tradeoffs: Gives users task-relevant language without splitting Data Management into separate products.
Requires task-specific capability and quality contracts, state normalization, task-specific review evidence, and focused runtime validation for currently shallow task paths.

consequences: Users must choose and learn separate Data Management workflows even though source selection, review, versioning, and publication are shared.
options.label: Option B — Separate task workflows
options.summary: Create a distinct checking and preparation workflow for every training task.
tradeoffs: Duplicates navigation, lifecycle, review, documentation, and testing across nine workflows.

consequences: The current confusion around rows, chunks, labels, boxes, masks, and generated examples would persist.
options.label: Option C — Generic common controls
options.summary: Keep universal check and preparation selectors with broad terminology.
tradeoffs: Cannot clearly express task-specific requirements or distinguish unsupported behavior.

discovery.summary: Data Ingestion has a sound staged-artifact, workspace, upload-validation, secure-egress, and provenance foundation, while Dataset Preparation has broad task and output coverage. The current end-to-end experience is not yet production-trustworthy: requested train/test ratios do not produce separate splits, the UI advertises input formats the worker cannot read, Hugging Face imports are remote Parquet registrations that require a separate localization step even though preparation cannot parse Parquet input, worker warnings are not surfaced, generation failures can log protected content, and the product lacks profiling, deduplication, privacy/license checks, leakage controls, human review, and versioned dataset documentation. The preparation form also exposes many model and data-engineering controls by default, which creates avoidable cognitive load for non-technical users.

research.summary: The approved architecture can support Increment 6 without a new host or persistence topology. The current shared source capability registry knows structured, document, and image formats, but it does not model input intent or method compatibility. Desktop and thin-client selectors still use three global presets; the desktop request builder always serializes character chunking and generation parameters, the thin client is hard-coded to instruction tuning, and the worker accepts combinations whose controls are ignored or change meaning. Advanced document processing ignores character overlap, requires preserved document boundaries, and uses character size only as an internal ceiling. Structured and image inputs bypass document chunking but can still carry document-centric advanced settings. The implementation should therefore add one contract-owned adaptive plan, serialize only active method fields, validate the same plan in application and worker boundaries, preserve exact source association, and render task/source-specific choices from that authority.
